content_voiceover: This slide shows how coagulation is activated at the site of vascular injury. When the endothelium is damaged, tissue factor is exposed on the subendothelial cells and on cells at the wound edge, shown here as step one. That tissue factor triggers the expression of a procoagulant phospholipid complex on the surface of activated cells, step two, which provides the anionic membrane surface that clotting factor complexes need to assemble efficiently. Step three is thrombin activation, where the assembled enzyme complexes convert prothrombin to thrombin in large amounts, and step four is fibrin polymerization, where thrombin cleaves fibrinogen into fibrin monomers that polymerize into the mesh you see holding the cellular elements together. Note that tissue factor is present on both sides of the wound, reinforcing that this is a bidirectional, localized response confined to the site of injury.
keypoints: Tissue factor exposed at injury site drives coagulation activation
Phospholipid complex expression provides the membrane surface for factor assembly
Fibrin polymerization stabilizes the platelet plug
keypoint_voiceover: Remember the four steps. Tissue factor exposure, phospholipid complex expression, thrombin activation, and fibrin polymerization, all happening locally at the site of vascular injury.
